relationship: Children dashed in judgment against Babylon
rationale: The psalm’s violent blessing concerning Babylon’s infants corresponds to Isaiah’s Babylon oracle describing their children dashed before them. Isaiah does not specify the psalm’s rock, and the comparison reports the texts rather than extending their command to another setting.

relationship: Human ways and tracks before God
rationale: God traced the speaker’s path and foresaw all his ways; Proverbs places a man’s ways before God’s eyes and says He watches all his tracks. The psalm’s measuring cord is not supplied to Proverbs.

relationship: Divine handholding and guidance
rationale: Both passages combine divine holding and guidance. Psalm 138 says God’s right hand holds the speaker; Psalm 72 says God grasped the speaker’s right hand and guided him in counsel.

relationship: Separation from sinners and men of blood
rationale: The source commands men of blood to turn away while addressing God concerning sinners; Psalm 25 asks not to have the speaker’s life destroyed together with ungodly people and men of bloodshed. Desired separation is shared, while the source’s conditional opening is preserved.

relationship: Declared hatred of God’s opponents or lawbreakers
rationale: Complete hatred of the Lord’s enemies can be compared with the declared hatred of lawbreakers alongside love of His law. The target identifies lawbreakers; it does not repeat the source’s complete-hatred wording.

relationship: Judgment for poor and needy people
rationale: The Lord’s action for the poor person’s judgment and needy people’s cause corresponds to the royal prayer for judgment of the poor and rescue of the children of the needy. The Lord and the king receiving His judgment are not treated as identical agents.

relationship: Prayer compared with incense and prayer at the incense hour
rationale: The comparison of prayer with incense can be read alongside the people praying at the hour when the priest burns incense. The psalm is a prayer-image, whereas Luke narrates simultaneous temple actions.

relationship: Eyes directed toward the Lord in dependence
rationale: The source directs its eyes toward the Lord and says it hoped in Him; Psalm 122 lifts eyes to Him and compares that attention with servants looking to their masters’ hands, continuing until divine compassion.

relationship: God’s good Spirit teaches and guides
rationale: The request to be taught God’s will and the affirmation that His good Spirit will lead the speaker correspond to the account of wilderness guidance and the gift of His good Spirit for understanding. Level ground is stated only in the psalm.

relationship: The Lord reigns for ever
rationale: The promise that the Lord will reign for ever corresponds to the song’s declaration that He reigns for ever and ever and beyond. Psalm 145 adds the address to Zion and every generation.

relationship: Goodness and beauty in the summons to praise
rationale: Psalm 146 commends praise because a psalm is good and asks that praise please God; Psalm 134 commands praise because the Lord is good and music because His name is beautiful. The differing subjects of good are preserved.

relationship: Horse and human strength contrasted with dependence on God
rationale: The Lord’s lack of delight in a horse’s might or human shins corresponds to the denial that great human force or a powerful horse saves. Divine pleasure and capacity to save are related contrasts, not the same assertion.

relationship: Ice and frost within divine rule over water
rationale: God casting ice like morsels and the question who withstands His cold correspond to Job’s questions about the origin of ice and frost and the fixing of the abyss’s face. The target’s actual flowing-water wording and questions are retained; it does not repeat the morsels image.

relationship: Divine breath or wind controls frost and water
rationale: The Lord’s sending His word to melt the ice and blowing wind so waters flow correspond to frost given from the Strong One’s breath and His steering water as He wishes. Frost-giving and melting are different actions.

relationship: A horn raised for God’s people or the righteous
rationale: Raising a horn of His people corresponds to the righteous person’s horns being raised alongside the promise to break sinners’ horns. The image is shared without identifying a particular ruler or event.

relationship: Questions about the Lord’s hearing
rationale: The assertion that the Lord Himself hears corresponds to the rhetorical question whether the One who planted the ear does not hear. This explains the shared hearing claim without assigning an unstated messenger to the source question.

relationship: David taken from the sheep and anointed
rationale: The account of being taken from the father’s sheep and anointed with oil corresponds to David summoned from the flock and anointed by Samuel. Psalm 151 names His angel while the Samuel narrative names Samuel; their identity is not resolved by the supported shepherd-to-anointing sequence.

relationship: Appearance does not secure the brothers’ election
rationale: The handsome and tall brothers in whom the Lord took no pleasure correspond to the warning not to regard Eliab’s appearance or height and the rejection of Jesse’s sons passing before Samuel. The narrative’s appearance warning is directed particularly at Eliab, not asserted of every brother.

relationship: David beheads the foreigner with the foreigner’s sword
rationale: Both passages describe David taking the opponent’s sword and removing his head. The psalm adds the removal of Israel’s reproach; the narrative records the foreigners fleeing when their champion died.

relationship: Silent music in mourning over Zion
rationale: Hanging the instruments amid Babylon’s captivity corresponds to chosen men ceasing from songs, joy ending and dancing turning to mourning because Mount Zion was destroyed. Lamentations does not mention willows or hung instruments; the specific link is the silence of music in the lament for Zion.

relationship: Sons compared with young plants
rationale: The source compares their sons to young plants established in youth; Psalm 127 compares sons to newly planted olive trees around the table. The source’s whose remains attached to its own context, and neither household nor daughter imagery is equated with the target’s wife and children.
